food.text: The Bengal famine of 1943 was the last major famine to affect areas within the modern Republic of India. Since then, threats of famine in 1984, 1988 and 1998 were contained by the Indian government, and there has been no major famine in India since 1943.

Indian Chinese cuisine grew from Chinese immigrants in British-ruled India, at places like Calcutta. Waves of Cantonese immigrants from Guangdong fled to India because of civil war, famine, poverty and conflict, and many opened restaurants and adapted their cooking to Indian tastes. By 2007, Chinese cuisine ranked as India's favourite cuisine after local food, growing at 9% annually.

The Bengal famine of 1943 resulted from many causes, including the Japanese occupation of Burma, which brought an influx of refugees and blocked Burmese grain imports. Other factors included grain and transport embargoes imposed by neighbouring provincial administrations, hoarding and profiteering by merchants, and a denial program that confiscated boats once used to move grain.
The Bihar drought of 1966 to 1967 gave impetus to further changes in agricultural policy in India. Those changes resulted in the Green Revolution.

In Karachi's Madrasi Para, a neighbourhood settled by Tamil Hindus who migrated in the early 20th century, South Indian food traditions endure. Dosa, made from a fermented batter of lentils and rice, takes about three days to prepare, including fermentation, and sells for around Rs500 ($3).

In the 20th and 21st centuries, Mughlai cuisine has been adapted by restaurants and roadside food stalls for a mass market. The result is a single dish of marinated chicken or meat cooked in a thick sauce based on tomato or cream, and accompanied by flatbreads or garnished rice dishes.

Bengal suffered a devastating famine from 1943 to 1944, and between 0.8 and 3.8 million people died of starvation. Among the causes the article lists are Japan's invasion of Burma, British export of food for the war in Europe, British denial orders that destroyed food transportation, and a ban on moving grain from other provinces, with offers of grain from Australia turned down. The British government denied an urgent request from Leopold Amery and Archibald Wavell to stop food exports from Bengal so the food could be used for famine relief. Winston Churchill dismissed the requests, which Amery regarded as "Hitler-like", by asking why, if the famine was so horrible, Gandhi had not yet died of starvation. His decision not to provide emergency food relief remains highly controversial.

Manchurian is said to have been invented in 1975 by Nelson Wang, who began with chopped garlic, ginger and green chillis. Instead of adding garam masala, he put in soy sauce, then cornstarch and the chicken. It bears little resemblance to traditional Manchu or Chinese cuisine.

In Ladakh, tea is traditionally made with strong green tea, butter and salt, mixed in a large churn. It is known as gurgur cha, after the sound it makes when mixed. Sweet tea made in the Indian style with milk and sugar is common now.

art.text: South Asian truck art is a popular form of decoration, with trucks covered in elaborate floral patterns and calligraphy. It is especially common in Pakistan and India. The tradition goes back to the 1920s, when trucks were imported into colonial India and locals began decorating them with age-old folk art.

The National Gallery of Modern Art was established on 29 March 1954 by the Government of India, at Jaipur House in New Delhi. Its collection holds more than 17,000 works by over 2000 artists. The Delhi branch, with 12,000 square meters of exhibition space, is one of the world's largest modern art museums.

India Art Fair, first held in 2008 as the India Art Summit, is India's largest art fair. It showcases modern and contemporary paintings, sculptures, photography, prints, drawings and video art. The first three editions drew a total of 146,000 visitors, making it one of the world's most popular art fairs.

The Art Deco movement of the early 20th century spread quickly to large parts of the world, including India. The Indian Institute of Architects, founded in Bombay in 1929, played a prominent role in propagating it. Indian architects were fascinated by the industrial modernity that Art Deco offered.

The Delhi Fine Arts Society was registered in 1929 and later became AIFACS. It was founded by the artist brothers Barada and Sarada Ukil, who were students of Abanindranath Tagore. In 1938 the group made the first proposal for a National Art Gallery, and in 1946 it organised the First International Contemporary Art Exhibition.

Prominent modernist buildings in India include IIM Ahmedabad by Louis Kahn (1961) and IIT Kanpur by Achyut Kanvinde (1963). IIM Bangalore by B. V. Doshi followed in 1973, and the Lotus Temple by Fariborz Sahba in 1986. Charles Correa designed Jawahar Kala Kendra in 1992.

Haider Ali is one of Pakistan's most prominent truck artists, trained by his father from his youth. He first came to international attention in 2002 when he painted a Pakistani truck as part of the Smithsonian Folklife Festival. Truck art has been called a big business in Pakistan, employing around 250,000 people in major centers as of 2014.

Since Indian independence in 1947, Karnataka has seen marked architectural changes. Tibetan refugees arrived in the state between 1963 and 1997, bringing traditional Tibetan art and architectural styles, as seen in the Buddhist monastery at Bylakuppe. Vidhana Soudha, built in Bangalore in 1953, reflects Neo-Dravidian influences that evolved after independence.

The 1949 Art Conference at Calcutta brought artists and critics together, including Stella Kramrisch, Nandalal Bose and Jamini Roy, to advise the government on art institutions. Historian Nihar Ranjan Ray urged the government to step in. Artist B. C. Sanyal argued it was wrong for the government to take the initiative away from artists.

Delhi-based truck artist Tilak Raj Dhir says the slogans he adds to his truck art often change with the socio-political atmosphere. Indian truck art commonly features eagles, kites and nazar battu, along with catchphrases like "Horn OK Please". Punjab is considered a major centre of the tradition.

In 2009, The Foxy Shahzadi, a 1974 VW Beetle decorated in a truck art style, travelled from Pakistan to France in a 25-day journey. Truck art has also inspired fashion, and Dolce & Gabbana used truck art-inspired displays in a 2015 campaign.

war.text: In the 1971 war, Pakistan's Eastern Command surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December 1971, thirteen days after fighting began. Approximately 93,000 Pakistani servicemen were taken prisoner by the Indian Army, and the surrender marked the formation of Bangladesh.

The 1965 war between India and Pakistan lasted seventeen days and caused thousands of casualties on both sides. According to the Library of Congress, Pakistan lost 3,800 troops, 200 tanks and twenty aircraft, and the article puts Indian army deaths at 3,000. It saw the largest engagement of armoured vehicles and the largest tank battle since World War II, and it ended with a ceasefire after the Soviet Union and the United States intervened diplomatically.

In March 1944 the Indian National Army, with Japanese help, crossed into India and advanced as far as Kohima in Nagaland. The Japanese finally retreated from the battles of Kohima and Imphal in June 1944, the farthest their advance reached on Indian territory. With little or no supplies, supply lines deluged by the monsoon and Allied aircraft harassing them, the INA's first division suffered a terrible fate in the withdrawal into Burma, as wounded, starved and diseased men succumbed along the way.

The first Kashmir war began on 22 October 1947, when tribal militias from Waziristan crossed into Jammu and Kashmir, with many Pakistani Army soldiers disguised as tribals among them. Instead of advancing on Srinagar, the raiders stayed in the captured border cities, looting and committing other crimes against the inhabitants, and records indicate the tribals beheaded many Hindu and Sikh civilians. Maharaja Hari Singh asked India for help, which was offered on condition that he sign the Instrument of Accession, and Indian troops were then airlifted to Srinagar.

India's forces in the 1971 war bypassed opposition and exploited weaknesses in Pakistani positions, which brought a swift victory. Faced with insurmountable losses, the Pakistani military capitulated in less than a fortnight, and panic spread through the Eastern Command's leadership. On 16 December 1971 the Indian Army encircled Dacca and issued a 30-minute ultimatum, and Lt-Gen. A.A.K. Niazi surrendered without resistance. According to CIA estimates, more than 3,500 Indian soldiers and about 5,000 Pakistani soldiers lost their lives, with tens of thousands wounded in total.

The Sino-Indian War of October to November 1962 was fought in two places about 1,000 km apart: the North-East Frontier Agency and Aksai Chin. India recognised the Johnson Line in the west and the McMahon Line in the east, while China recognised neither.

India's operation of 1984 to capture the Siachen Glacier was called Operation Meghdoot. India took the 70-kilometre-long glacier and the main passes of the Saltoro Ridge, including Sia La, Bilafond La and Gyong La. A cease-fire began in 2003, but both sides still keep a heavy military presence there.

India Gate stands in New Delhi as a memorial to 74,187 Indian Army soldiers who died between 1914 and 1921. They fell in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War, in places from France and Flanders to Mesopotamia and Gallipoli. Edwin Lutyens designed it in the style of Roman triumphal arches.

Pakistan's Operation Chengiz Khan opened the 1971 war with preemptive aerial strikes on eight Indian air stations. The strikes led India to declare war on Pakistan and to enter the conflict on the side of Bengali nationalist forces.

The Amar Jawan Jyoti, a black marble plinth with a reversed rifle capped by a war helmet, was built beneath India Gate after the 1971 war. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi inaugurated it on 26 January 1972. It has served as India's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

After the 1965 war, India drew closer to the Soviet Union, which became its biggest supplier of military hardware. From 1967 to 1977, 81% of India's arms imports came from the Soviet Union. The shift followed frustration that the United States did little to stop Pakistan's use of American arms.

In March 1943 Lieutenant-General Renya Mutaguchi took command of Japan's Fifteenth Army in Burma and forcefully advocated invading India from the moment he did. He may have been goaded by the first Chindit expedition, led by Orde Wingate. The Allies widely publicised its successes while concealing their losses to disease and exhaustion, possibly leading Mutaguchi and some of his staff to underestimate the difficulties ahead. Those difficulties ended in catastrophe: of 54,879 Japanese casualties at Imphal and Kohima, 13,376 were dead, most from starvation, disease and exhaustion.

The Japanese Indian Ocean raid ran from 31 March to 10 April 1942. It was only partially successful, but it forced the British fleet to relocate from Ceylon to Kilindini at Mombasa in Kenya, because forward anchorages could not be protected.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

literature.text: India's Constitution officially recognises 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, while the Sahitya Akademi, India's highest literary body, recognises 24 literary languages. Konkani is one of the few Indian languages written in five scripts: Roman, Nagari, Kannada, Persian-Arabic and Malayalam.

In 1913 and 1914, the Hindustan Ghadar press in San Francisco published Ghadar di Gunj, a collection of nationalist and socialist songs and poems in Gurumukhi and Shahmukhi. The British Indian government deemed related pamphlets, including Ghadar di Goonj and Talwar, seditionist and banned them from publication and circulation in India.

Nissim Ezekiel is considered a pioneering figure in modern Indian English poetry. His first book, A Time to Change, was published in 1952, and poets of his time included A. K. Ramanujan, R. Parthasarathy, Kamala Das and Arun Kolatkar.

Khamba Thoibi Sheireng is a Meitei epic poem of 39,000 lines, the third longest Indian epic poem after the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. It is based on the classic tale of Khamba and Thoibi and is regarded as the national epic of the Manipuris.

Muhammad Iqbal's Bang-e-Dara, published in 1924, is a collection of Urdu poetry written in three distinct phases of his life. The poems he wrote up to 1905 blend Persian mysticism with Indian patriotism and include Tarana-e-Hind, popularly known as Saare Jahan Se Achcha.

R. Parthasarathy edited Ten Twentieth-Century Indian Poets, published by Oxford University Press in 1976. He also translated the fifth-century Tamil epic The Tale of the Anklet into modern English verse, published by Columbia University Press in 1993. It won the Sahitya Akademi Translation Prize in 1995.

Pandey Bechan Sharma's 1924 story collection Chocolate focused on male homosexuality and sparked debate. Many in the Hindi writing sphere condemned it, led by Banarsidas Chaturvedi, and the 1953 edition added several forewords arguing the book intended to condemn homosexuality.
In 1973, Kamala Das began publishing her autobiography My Story in Malayalam, which included frank depictions of her same-sex desires. The work was popular and caused large controversy.
R. Parthasarathy's Rough Passage, published by Oxford University Press in 1977, is a long poem. In his preface he describes it as a book where all the poems form part of a single poem.
In 1936, Urdu poet Firaaq Gorakhpuri defended same-sex love as a universal phenomenon in an essay on ghazals. This inspired more Urdu poetry with homosexual themes.

Sahitya Akademi prizes for English poetry have gone to Nissim Ezekiel for Latter-Day Psalms in 1983 and Kamala Das for Collected Poems in 1985. A. K. Ramanujan won for Collected Poems in 1999, and Dom Moraes won for Serendip in 1994.

science.text: After independence, Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, initiated reforms to promote higher education and science and technology. The first Indian Institute of Technology was inaugurated on 18 August 1951 at Kharagpur in West Bengal. More IITs soon followed in Bombay, Madras, Kanpur and Delhi.

Close ties with the Soviet Union beginning in the 1960s enabled ISRO to rapidly develop the Indian space program and advance nuclear power in India. India carried out its first nuclear test explosion on 18 May 1974 at Pokhran.

All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi, was established under the AIIMS Act of 1956, and the bill was adopted in May 1956. It is regarded as one of the best public medical research universities and hospitals in India. It ranked first among Indian medical colleges in the National Institutional Ranking Framework in 2024.
science.source_title: All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi

science.text: The Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology in Nilore, Islamabad, was designed by American architect Edward Durell Stone and completed in 1965. It has been described as possibly the most architecturally stunning physics complex in the world.
science.source_title: Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology

science.text: The Indian Institute of Technology was conceived by a 22-member committee of scholars and entrepreneurs to promote technical education. It was inaugurated by the education minister, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Regional Engineering Colleges, now National Institutes of Technology, were opened in the same period.

India increased its output of scientific papers fourfold between 2000 and 2015, overtaking Russia and France in the absolute number of papers per year. In the quality-adjusted Nature Index, India ranked ninth worldwide in 2023 and grew faster than China that year, though from a lower base.

PINSTECH grew out of the Atoms for Peace initiative in 1953 and the efforts of Abdus Salam, who had lobbied for a professional physics laboratory since 1951. He wanted scientists from developing countries to interact with peers from industrial nations without permanently leaving home. Construction began after he found funding from the United States in 1961.
science.source_title: Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology

science.text: In 1965 the Comprehensive Rural Health Services Project was set up at Ballabgarh in Haryana with a 50-bed hospital. It followed a Rural Field Practice established at AIIMS Delhi in 1961 with help from the Rockefeller Foundation. The site later became the Ballabgarh Health and Demographic Surveillance System.
science.source_title: All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi

science.text: After the costly 1971 war with India, PINSTECH was repurposed from its original civilian mission into a primary weapons laboratory, though it was never intended to be a nuclear physics or weapons laboratory. Its tiny research reactor could never be a source of weapons-grade plutonium, and plutonium pit production was difficult at first. In 1973 its scientists began producing plutonium oxide and uranium oxide, and the lab gave Pakistani scientists a ground to design and engineer weapon designs, with many feared that India was rapidly developing a nuclear bomb. Its New Labs facility produced the first batch of weapon-grade plutonium (239Pu) by 1983, the source material for the nuclear test at the Ras Koh Range on 30 May 1998.
science.source_title: Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology

science.text: PINSTECH's study of uranium hexafluoride chemistry led to technology transfer to the Islamabad Uranium Conversion Facility in 1974. It also led to the production of Zircaloys, first made at the lab. That technology was later transferred to the Kundian Nuclear Fuel Complex in 1980.
science.source_title: Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science & Technology

politics.text: The British Raj, the direct rule of the British Crown over the Indian subcontinent, lasted from 1858 to 1947. It ended when the territory was partitioned into two sovereign dominions, the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan. In border areas millions of Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs relocated across the new borders, and in Punjab, where the border divided the Sikh regions in half, there was much bloodshed. Somewhere between 250,000 and 500,000 people on both sides of the borders died in the violence. Pakistan later split again, when Bangladesh was proclaimed independent in 1971.

When the Second World War began, India's Congress party demanded independence before it would help Britain. London refused, and when Congress launched its "Quit India" campaign in August 1942, the government immediately arrested over 60,000 national and local Congress leaders. It then moved to suppress the violent reaction of Congress supporters. Key leaders were kept in prison until June 1945, while the Muslim League and the Hindu Mahasabha supported the British war effort.

In late 1946, Britain's Labour government decided to end British rule of India. In early 1947 it announced that it intended to transfer power no later than June 1948. It also planned to take part in forming an interim government.

The Forty-second Amendment of 1976 asserted the Preamble to the Constitution of India as secular. In the 1994 case S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, the Supreme Court established that India had been secular since the Republic was formed on 26 January 1950.
tags: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India

politics.text: In September 1939 the Viceroy, the Marquess of Linlithgow, declared war on Germany on India's behalf. Elements of the Indian National Congress criticised him for not consulting the Indian people. Congress was then the largest and most influential political party in India.

In February 1946 the Royal Indian Navy mutinied in Bombay, followed by others in Calcutta, Madras and Karachi. Although the mutinies were rapidly suppressed, they spurred Britain's new Labour government to action. The result was the Cabinet Mission to India, led by Lord Pethick Lawrence and including Sir Stafford Cripps.
Indian law treats all native religions as falling broadly under Hinduism. The 1955 Hindu Marriage Act defines as Hindus anyone who is not a Christian, Muslim, or Jew.

Japan set up the Indian National Army under Subhas Chandra Bose. It began with prisoners taken in Malaya and at Singapore, who were offered the choice of serving in it or remaining in very poor conditions in POW camps. On 21 October 1943 Japan gave nominal control of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the Provisional Government of Free India, which controlled no Indian territory and was used only to raise troops for Japan. In March 1944 the army crossed into India and advanced as far as Kohima. When the siege of Imphal was broken, its first division withdrew with little or no supplies, harassed by Allied air dominance, and wounded, starved and diseased men succumbed during the retreat into Burma.

Krushna Chandra Gajapati, Maharaja of Paralakhemundi, is regarded as the architect of an independent united Odisha. He became the first Prime Minister of Orissa province, formed in 1936. He served from 1 April 1937 to 19 July 1937, and again from 29 November 1941 to 29 June 1944.

Political identity organisations multiplied in the early 20th century. Sikhs founded the Shiromani Akali Dal in 1920, and the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh was formed in 1925–1926. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, tried to keep its distance from such socio-religious movements and identity politics.

The last Maharaja of Tripura's Manikya dynasty, Bir Bikram Kishore, chose to join the predominantly Hindu Dominion of India in 1947. The final accession was signed by his widow, Kanchan Prava Devi, in place of the minor Kirit Bikram Kishore. This ended five centuries of Manikya rule.

Porbandar was a 13-Gun Salute State of British India ruled by the Jethwa dynasty. Its last ruler, Rana Natwarsinhji, signed the Instrument of Accession to the Union of India on 15 August 1947. He died in 1979, and because his crown prince had died in 1977, the throne was left vacant.

The Thondaiman dynasty ruled the Pudukkottai region from the 17th to the 20th century. Its rule did not end at Indian Independence: the Pudukottai Samasthanam remained under the dynasty for one year even after independence.

philosophy.text: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was a philosopher who served as Vice President of India from 1952 to 1962 and then as President of India from 1962 to 1967. His philosophy was grounded in Advaita Vedanta, which he reinterpreted for a contemporary understanding.

Radhakrishnan defended Hinduism against what he called uninformed Western criticism, helping to shape contemporary Hindu identity. He influenced how Hinduism is understood in both India and the west, and earned a reputation as a bridge-builder between India and the West.

Secularism in India is understood to mean not a complete separation of religion from state, but a state that participates in a neutral manner in the affairs of all religious groups, and of atheism, while keeping equidistance from all. The Preamble to the Constitution of India states that India is a secular state.

Radhakrishnan held the King George V Chair of Mental and Moral Science at the University of Calcutta from 1921 to 1932. He later held the Spalding Chair of Eastern Religion and Ethics at the University of Oxford from 1936 to 1952.

When Radhakrishnan arrived in Calcutta in 1921, some of the Bengali intellectual elite resented a southerner holding the most important chair of philosophy in India. The Modern Review, which criticised the appointment of non-Bengalis, became the main vehicle of criticism.

In the January 1929 issue of The Modern Review, the philosopher Jadunath Sinha claimed that his teacher Radhakrishnan had copied parts of Sinha's 1922 doctoral thesis into Indian Philosophy II. Sinha presented 110 instances of borrowings in letters exchanged in the journal.

Radhakrishnan replied that he and Sinha had both used the same classical texts and standard translations, so similarities were unavoidable. He added that he lectured on the subject before publishing, and that his book was ready in 1924, before Sinha's thesis was published.

culture.text: Cricket is by far the most popular sport in India. The national team won the 1983 Cricket World Cup and the 2011 Cricket World Cup. The Board conducts the Indian Premier League, a Twenty20 competition.

India is the birthplace of four major world religions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. Together they represent about 83% of India's population. India also has the largest populations of Zoroastrians and followers of the Bahá'í Faith in the world.

Arranged marriages have long been the norm in Indian society, and most Indians still have their marriages planned by their parents and respected family members. According to the 2011 Census of India, the average age of marriage for women had risen to 21 years. In 2009, about 7% of women married before the age of 18.

Rajiv Gandhi announced most of India's zonal cultural centres in 1985, and they began functioning in 1986 to 1987. They serve seven overlapping cultural zones defined by the Ministry of Culture. Their stated goal is to strengthen the ancient roots of Indian culture and enrich a composite national culture.

Indian cinema has increasingly portrayed LGBTQ lives with nuance. The 2019 film Ek Ladki Ko Dekha Toh Aisa Laga, starring Sonam Kapoor, was celebrated as a landmark for depicting a mainstream lesbian romance. In 2022, Priyakanta Laishram's ONENESS became the first gay-themed movie from Northeast India.
tags: Ek Ladki Ko Dekha Toh Aisa Laga

culture.text: The 2011 census listed atheists, Zoroastrians, Jews and tribal religions under Other Religions and Persuasions, about 7.9 million people in all. The most numerous of these groupings were Sarna with 4.9 million respondents and Gondi with 1 million.

Since 1956, Indian laws treat males and females as equal in inheritance without a legal will. Historically, family estates passed down the male line, and the dowry was traditionally considered a woman's share of family wealth. By 2004, about 20 percent of Indians used a legal will for inheritance.

The 2011 census listed about 7.9 million people under "Other Religions and Persuasions", outside the main religious communities. The most numerous group was Sarna, with 4.9 million respondents, followed by Gondi with 1 million. Others included Sari Dharam, Donyi-Poloism, Sanamahi and Khasi.

In 2011, India inaugurated its first motor racing circuit, the privately built Buddh International Circuit in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The 5.14-kilometre track hosted the first Formula One Indian Grand Prix in October 2011.

Early LGBTQ networking in India relied on mailing lists such as the Khush-list, established in 1993, and GayBombay, established in 1998. Qradio, launched in 2013, became India's first 24-hour radio station dedicated to an LGBT audience. In 2012, Madurai hosted Asia's first specific genderqueer pride parade.
